extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, judges, and legal scholars (U.S. practice; historical statutes)
extracted.subtask_description: Legal rules and standards governing (1) extensions of patent terms (statutory and Patent Office extensions), including who may apply, timing, grounds, and the effect of extension certificates; and (2) acquisition and transfer of title to patents (occupancy, assignments, special tenures, recording, and related limits). Primarily discusses U.S. doctrine under 19th-century statutes and case law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible term of Congressional extensions
rubrics_metrics.description: Congressional extensions are usually granted for seven years but may lawfully be granted for any limited length of time, whether longer or shorter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Special acts may specify any limited duration; courts will read the certificate of extension in light of the statute even if the certificate omits recital of statutory limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of special-extension statutes
rubrics_metrics.description: Some special acts simply extend patent duration by legislative edict; others authorize the Commissioner to ascertain facts and decide whether extension should be granted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an extension is authorized by statute delegating fact-finding to the Commissioner, the certificate need not recite the limiting provisions of the special act because the law reads the certificate in light of that statute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finality of Congressional-extension validity
rubrics_metrics.description: Special Acts of Congress granting or authorizing extensions are subject to the general rule that the validity of a statute cannot be questioned in courts on allegations that its passage was procured by fraud or bribery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such acts are treated as engrafted on general patent laws and construed in connection with them; courts will not question legislative validity for alleged procurement fraud.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent Office extension authorization and repeal history
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent Office extensions were authorized by the Patent Act of July 4, 1836, prohibited for future patents by the Act of March 3, 1861, with later re-enactments for patents granted before March 2, 1861.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical context affects availability of Patent Office extensions; applicability depends on date of grant and statutory reenactments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application formalities for Patent Office extensions (1836 statute)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patentee desiring an extension must apply in writing to the Commissioner, setting forth the grounds; pay the fee; notice of application must be published specifying time and place for consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under 1836 statute the Secretary of State, Commissioner, and Solicitor constituted a board to hear evidence; later statutes vested decision in the Commissioner alone but retained hearing/notice features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounds for Patent Office extension (meritorious facts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Extension meritorious if, without fault or neglect by the inventor-patentee, he failed to obtain from use and sale of the invention a reasonable remuneration for the time, ingenuity, expense and for its introduction into public use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These facts had to appear to the satisfaction of the Commissioner; once the Commissioner grants an extension, courts in infringement suits will not admit evidence showing those facts did not in fact exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect and term of Patent Office extensions
rubrics_metrics.description: When extension granted under statute, Commissioner must extend patent by certificate for seven years from after expiration of the first term; extended patent has same legal effect as if originally granted for twenty-one years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statute also forbade granting an extension after expiration of the original term.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing to file application for extension (post-1870 rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under statutes of 1870 and the Revised Statutes, application had to be filed not more than six months nor less than ninety days before expiration of the original term.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jurisdiction to consider extension depends on filing and fee payment in the statutory window to allow the Commissioner to investigate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may apply for an extension — 'patentee' vs inventor/assignee
rubrics_metrics.description: Statutes specified 'patentees' as entitled to apply, but where inventor had an equitable interest he could properly apply alone; when inventor would have no equitable interest no extension could be obtained for the sole benefit of others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an assignee holds legal title, the inventor may still apply if he would receive an equitable interest; assignment and equitable interests must be assessed case-by-case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executor/administrator and joint inventor rules for applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Executor or administrator of an inventor-patentee may apply for an extension; joint inventors must all join in an application if all are living, and legal representatives must join for deceased inventors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These principles derive from case law (e.g., Wilson v. Rousseau) and were adjudicated by courts.

rubrics_metrics.name: No extensions after expiration of original term
rubrics_metrics.description: No Patent Office extension is grantable after the expiration of the original term; extensions must be granted prior to midnight of the last day of the original term.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rule applies even where patents are limited by foreign patent dates; extensions tied to the relevant expiration (e.g., foreign patent expiry in some circumstances).

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdiction acquisition for extension proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Commissioner's jurisdiction was acquired when the proper person filed an application and paid the requisite fee, provided the application and fee were filed in sufficient time to permit investigation (and within the statutory window after July 8, 1870).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commissioner's decision regarding jurisdiction was never conclusive; courts may review the question but give great weight to the practical construction by the executive charged with execution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Directory (non-jurisdictional) nature of procedural requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Statutory requirements that the Commissioner advertise applications, refer to the principal examiner, and hold hearings are directory and not jurisdictional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Omissions or irregular performance of these acts do not affect the validity of an extension in infringement suits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fraud allegations against extensions require special proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Allegations of fraud practiced upon or by the Commissioner in securing or granting an extension cannot be inquired into collaterally in infringement suits; such grave charges must be pursued in a special proceeding to repeal the grant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collateral allegations of inadvertence, error or ministerial irregularity are similarly limited; fraud charges deserve a direct proceeding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certificate of extension — form and effect
rubrics_metrics.description: The statutory certificate of extension was generally indorsed on the original letters patent; if the original is lost or unavailable, indorsement on a certified copy is equally valid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The certificate is to be read in light of the authorizing statute; the Commissioner's indorsement is evidence he was satisfied of required facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment of inchoate patent and extension rights
rubrics_metrics.description: An inchoate right (right between invention and issuance) to a patent or to a Patent Office extension is assignable; such an assignment conveys legal title to the letters patent or extension as soon as they are granted, even if the assignment did not request issuance in the assignee's name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rule applies to assignments executed or recorded before or after grant; assignments of pending applications likewise convey the whole interest (legal and equitable).

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal title transfer formalities — writing required
rubrics_metrics.description: Assignments of legal title to patents must be in writing because statute provides no other method; patent rights are statutory and transfer of legal title must follow statutory form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equitable title, by contrast, may be created or transferred by parol. Recitals that someone is an owner without proper form do not create even an equitable assignment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements for a sufficient assignment description
rubrics_metrics.description: An assignment should describe the patent by number, date, patentee name, and invention name; however, an assignment is valid if its description excludes doubt as to the patent intended even if particulars are lacking or erroneous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Broad conveyances ('all the property... including patents, trade marks') can be effective despite inability to record; but an assignment of a machine patent will not convey a process patent solely useful in performance of that machine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special tenures and conditional assignments
rubrics_metrics.description: Assignments may create titles held upon special tenures (e.g., condition to pay royalties, to manufacture sufficient articles, to sell proceeds to assignor, or to refrain from assigning/licensing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conditions should be stated in the assignment but may be in a separate unrecorded paper effective between parties (but not binding on purchasers without notice). Burden of proving non-compliance rests on the party asserting it; proven non-compliance (absent intervening rights) causes title to revert to assignor. Non-payment of purchase notes may cause reversion while notes remain due.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rights of licensees/assignees during extended term
rubrics_metrics.description: The benefit of an extension extends to assignees and grantees to the extent of their interest: a person who at the beginning of an extended term had a right to use a particular specimen had the same right during the extended term, unless expressly limited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limitations: (1) applies only to rights existing at beginning of extension (patentee can make licenses expire before extension); (2) does not confer rights to make new specimens; (3) does not apply to process patents; (4) does not create rights not existing before extension (royalties continue); (5) confers right to repair but not to manufacture new articles; (6) does not apply where original grant expressly limited to existing term. The right is property and transferable by sale, devise or assignment in insolvency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical effect of Commissioner's satisfaction
rubrics_metrics.description: The statute required that the Commissioner be satisfied of the meritorious facts for extension; evidence that such facts did not in fact exist was inadmissible in infringement suits once an extension had been granted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This protects extensions granted on the Commissioner's satisfaction from collateral attack in infringement litigation; direct proceedings are required for annulment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignments in blank and estoppel
rubrics_metrics.description: Persons who execute assignments in blank are estopped from denying propriety of the filled assignment when invoked by purchasers for value who lacked notice of fraud or error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protects innocent purchasers and provides an equitable estoppel against the original assignor in appropriate circumstances.
